Benefits of eating that entity:
1) One of the richest natural sources of Vitamin C, boosting immunity.
2) High calcium supports strong bones and teeth.
3) High fiber content aids digestion.
How much to eat per day: 1-2 teaspoons (~5-10g) of the powdery pulp mixed in water, milk, or a smoothie, a few times a week (not eaten as a whole 'wet' fruit - the pulp is naturally dry).

Nutritious Components: Very low calorie small berry (~5-10 kcal per berry); limited standardized 100g nutrition data exists since it's eaten in tiny amounts. Contains 'miraculin', a natural protein that temporarily makes sour foods taste sweet.
Benefits of eating that entity:
1) Fun, safe way to make naturally sour fruits (like lemons) taste sweet without added sugar.
2) Can encourage kids to try more fruits and less added sugar.
3) A great, safe science-of-taste lesson for students.
How much to eat per day: 1-2 berries at a time (chewed, not swallowed whole), occasionally - it is a flavor-changer, not a fruit eaten for bulk nutrition.

Nutritious Components: 99 kcal | Carbs 25g | Protein 1.5g | Vitamin C ~2.7mg | Niacin and Beta-Carotene (notable)
Benefits of eating that entity:
1) Naturally sweet flavor (tastes like sweet potato/maple) without needing added sugar.
2) Beta-carotene supports healthy eyes and skin.
3) Good source of dietary fiber for digestion.
How much to eat per day: 1 small fruit or 2-3 tablespoons of pulp (~50g), occasionally, often used blended in smoothies.

Nutritious Components: ~74 kcal | Carbs ~18g | Protein ~1.6g | Vitamin C ~20mg (estimate) | Potassium (notable)
Benefits of eating that entity:
1) Unique tropical flavor (tastes like a mix of pineapple and banana).
2) Good source of Vitamin C and potassium.
3) Fun way to learn about unusual tropical plants.
How much to eat per day: A few small pieces (~50g) ONLY when fully ripe (skin/scales fall off on their own) - the unripe fruit contains sharp calcium oxalate crystals that can irritate the mouth/throat, so an adult should always check ripeness first.

Nutritious Components: ~47 kcal | Carbs ~11g | Protein ~1-2g | Vitamin C ~100-150mg
Benefits of eating that entity:
1) High Vitamin C content supports the immune system.
2) Traditionally used across the Pacific and Asia for general wellness.
3) Good source of potassium for muscle function.
How much to eat per day: A small amount only (1-2 tsp of juice diluted in water) - the ripe fruit has a very strong smell/taste and is usually consumed as diluted juice, not eaten whole.

Nutritious Components: ~115-145 kcal (cured/brined, as typically eaten) | Carbs ~6g | Protein ~0.8g | Fat ~11-15g (mostly healthy monounsaturated fat) | Vitamin E ~1.7mg
Benefits of eating that entity:
1) Healthy monounsaturated fats are good for the heart.
2) Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant for skin and cells.
3) Adds flavor to meals in a way that's more nutritious than fried snacks.
How much to eat per day: 4-6 olives (~15-20g) at a time - raw olives straight off the tree are very bitter and are always cured/brined before eating, and can be high in salt, so should be enjoyed in small amounts.

Nutritious Components: ~55 kcal (estimate) | Carbs ~12g | Protein ~0.7g | Vitamin C (good source, exact value not well standardized in food databases)
Benefits of eating that entity:
1) A traditional Himalayan wild fruit rich in antioxidants.
2) Good source of Vitamin C for immunity.
3) Naturally sweet-tart taste with minerals like calcium and potassium.
How much to eat per day: A small handful (~30-40g) as a seasonal fresh treat (has a very short shelf life of 2-3 days).

Nutritious Components: ~52 kcal (estimate, based on related raspberry species) | Carbs ~12g | Protein ~1.2g | Vitamin C ~26mg (estimate)
Benefits of eating that entity:
1) Rich in fiber, good for digestion.
2) Vitamin C content supports the immune system.
3) Antioxidant pigments help protect the body's cells.
How much to eat per day: A small handful (~40-50g) fresh, in season - a wild Himalayan berry best eaten fresh as it spoils quickly.

Nutritious Components: Very limited standardized nutrition data available for this wild Himalayan fruit; broadly similar in composition to other small wild berries (~45-55 kcal, moderate Vitamin C, per 100g, as an estimate).
Benefits of eating that entity:
1) A traditional wild-foraged fruit valued in local hill communities.
2) Likely provides fiber and antioxidants typical of wild berries.
3) A good way to learn about regional/local biodiversity.
How much to eat per day: A small handful (~30g), only when identified and given by a knowledgeable adult, as wild berries should always be correctly identified before eating.

Nutritious Components: ~76 kcal | Carbs ~20g | Protein ~0.4g | Vitamin C ~8mg
Benefits of eating that entity:
1) Good source of fiber for healthy digestion.
2) Contains natural plant antioxidants (like regular apples).
3) Tart flavor is often turned into healthy jams/chutneys.
How much to eat per day: 1 small fruit (~50-60g); usually cooked into jam or chutney since raw crab apples are very tart.

Nutritious Components: ~60 kcal | Carbs ~12g | Protein ~1.3g | Vitamin C ~28mg | Lycopene (exceptionally high - more than tomatoes)
Benefits of eating that entity:
1) Contains far more lycopene than tomatoes, a strong antioxidant.
2) Good Vitamin C content for immunity.
3) Tangy-sweet wild berry that's a great way to explore local fruits.
How much to eat per day: A small handful (~30-40g) fresh when fully ripe (red and slightly soft) - unripe berries are very astringent.

Nutritious Components: ~50 kcal (estimate) | Carbs ~11g | Vitamin C (moderate-good, exact standardized value limited)
Benefits of eating that entity:
1) Traditionally valued for its tart, Vitamin-C-rich berries.
2) Contains natural antioxidant plant pigments.
3) A good example of traditional Himalayan food and medicine plants.
How much to eat per day: A small handful (~20-30g) - the berries are quite sour/tart and usually eaten in small quantities or made into chutney.

Nutritious Components: Nutrition data on the edible pulp is very limited, as this tree (Schleichera oleosa) is grown mainly for the oil pressed from its seeds rather than for eating the fruit pulp itself.
Benefits of eating that entity:
1) The thin sweet-sour pulp around the seed is eaten fresh by local communities.
2) The tree plays an important ecological role (also hosts lac insects).
3) A good example of how one plant can serve many different uses.
How much to eat per day: A very small amount of pulp (a few grams) as a local, occasional treat - this fruit is not a significant everyday food source.

Benefits of eating that entity:
1) Outstanding source of Vitamin C for strong immunity.

3) Rich in antioxidants that support overall health.
How much to eat per day: 1 small-medium fruit or a small glass of fresh juice (~100ml), occasionally - the astringent (tannin) taste means many prefer it as juice; avoid the toxic raw cashew nut shell entirely.

Benefits of eating that entity:
1) Provides quick natural energy, great for active kids.
2) Good fiber content supports healthy digestion.
3) Contains potassium and iron for overall growth.
How much to eat per day: 2-3 fresh fruits (~40-50g) as a natural-sugar snack.

Nutritious Components: Very limited standardized nutrition data available for this Northeast Indian wild fruit (Calamus species); broadly similar to other sour wild fruits (rich in Vitamin C, low calorie, as an estimate).
Benefits of eating that entity:
1) A traditional wild fruit enjoyed by communities in Northeast India.
2) Likely a natural source of Vitamin C, like other sour wild fruits.
3) A good way to learn about India's diverse regional foods.
How much to eat per day: A very small amount (a few pieces), typically eaten with salt/chili as a local snack - best given by someone familiar with the fruit.

Nutritious Components: ~79 kcal (estimate, based on the related jujube/ber family) | Carbs ~20g | Protein ~1.2g | Vitamin C ~40mg (jujubes are notably Vitamin-C rich)
Benefits of eating that entity:
1) Good natural source of Vitamin C.
2) Provides quick, healthy natural energy.
3) A wild relative of the common ber (Indian jujube) fruit that kids may already know.
How much to eat per day: A small handful (~30-40g) fresh, when ripe.

Benefits of eating that entity:
1) A lesser-known regional wild fruit valued by local communities.
2) Likely provides fiber, like most small wild fruits.
3) Helps students learn about lesser-known Indian biodiversity.
How much to eat per day: A small amount, only when identified and offered by a knowledgeable adult.

Benefits of eating that entity:
1) Wild figs are generally a good source of fiber for digestion.
2) Provide calcium that supports bone growth.
3) A good example of India's lesser-known native fig species.
How much to eat per day: A small handful (~30-40g) when fully ripe and soft.

1) Higher protein content than most fruits.
2) Traditionally used in regional Indian cooking and pickles.
3) A good way to explore lesser-known desert and dryland foods of India.
How much to eat per day: A very small amount (a few berries, ~10-15g), usually eaten pickled or cooked rather than raw, occasionally.

Benefits of eating that entity:
1) Like other citrus fruits, likely a good natural source of Vitamin C.
2) Its strong aroma and sourness make it useful in small amounts to flavor food naturally.
3) A good way to learn about India's wild citrus relatives.

1) Good natural source of quick energy.
2) Contains antioxidants similar to its cousin, the rambutan.
3) Sweet, juicy flesh makes it an enjoyable way to try new tropical fruits.
How much to eat per day: 3-4 fruits (~80-100g) as an occasional snack, spitting out the seed.

Nutritious Components: The fleshy green husk surrounding the macadamia nut is usually discarded and has very limited standardized nutrition data, as almost all nutrition research focuses on the nut kernel inside, not the outer pulp.
Benefits of eating that entity:
1) The husk is mainly of ecological/composting value rather than a food source.
2) The nut inside (once shelled) is the truly nutritious, healthy-fat-rich part of this plant.
3) A good example of how not every part of a fruit plant is meant to be eaten.
How much to eat per day: The husk/pulp itself is not typically eaten by people - only the shelled nut inside is a food (and nuts should be given in small amounts due to their richness).

Benefits of eating that entity:

2) A fun way to see where chocolate actually comes from.
3) Contains antioxidant plant compounds.
How much to eat per day: A small handful of the fresh white pulp (~30-40g) sucked off the seeds as a treat - the raw seeds themselves are bitter and are not eaten directly (they're processed into cocoa/chocolate).

2) Very low in calories for the nutrition it provides.
3) Vivid red-orange colour makes it a fun 'superfood' to learn about.
How much to eat per day: A few tablespoons of the aril (~20-30g), usually cooked briefly (e.g., in Vietnamese sticky rice) rather than eaten raw.

Benefits of eating that entity:

2) Provides a decent amount of Vitamin C for immunity.
3) Its custard-like sweet flesh is an enjoyable way to try new tropical fruits.
